title: Knowledge check: XML Parsing in Browsers

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly covered in “XML Parsing in Browsers”?
questions.explanation: The attached XML curriculum lists “Parsing XML in web applications” under lesson 117, “XML Parsing in Browsers”. The other options are from different topics or unrelated areas.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the most reliable rule to remember when applying “XML Parsing in Browsers”?
options: A namespace prefix is an alias; the namespace name identifies the vocabulary.
Indentation always changes the data model.
Well-formed XML is automatically valid against every schema.
Every XML processor supports every version of XSLT and XPath.
questions.answer_key: A namespace prefix is an alias; the namespace name identifies the vocabulary.
questions.explanation: The correct choice separates the relevant XML concepts and avoids assumptions about processor behavior. Check the linked standard and actual implementation for details.

questions.prompt: After creating an example for “XML Parsing in Browsers”, what is the best next step?
options: Verify a normal case, an invalid or boundary case, and document the tool/version used.
Rely on visual appearance without parsing or validation.
Change several parts at once and infer the cause if the result changes.
questions.answer_key: Verify a normal case, an invalid or boundary case, and document the tool/version used.
questions.explanation: A small, reproducible test suite distinguishes expected behavior from a lucky example and makes version assumptions visible.

notes: Answer keys and explanations remain in the server-side course repository; API GET responses expose only prompts/options and submit responses reveal feedback after grading.
